title: Caldo Tlalpeno
subtitle: chipotle and chickpea broth with chicken, from Mexico City
excerpt: Caldo tlalpeno is a smoky, warming broth from the outskirts of Mexico City. Chipotle chillies give it colour and gentle heat. Chickpeas and shredded chicken make it filling enough for a main meal.
sourceNotes: Caldo tlalpeno takes its name from Tlalpan, a borough on the outskirts of Mexico City. The soup was historically served at roadside inns on the route between the capital and Tlalpan. It is a light but warming broth suited to any time of year.

glossaryTerms.definition: A smoke-dried jalapeño chilli. Chipotle in adobo refers to chipotles sold tinned in a tangy tomato and vinegar sauce. They add smokiness and moderate heat.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes 55 minutes from start to finish. The broth gets its depth from

chillies in adobo sauce and a tin of crushed tomatoes. Chicken thighs poach directly in the broth, then get shredded and returned. A 400g tin of drained chickpeas goes in for the last 10 minutes to warm through and absorb the smoky flavour.

Start with two chipotle chillies from the tin and add more adobo sauce rather than more chillies if you want a smokier flavour without extra heat. The adobo sauce carries a lot of the flavour and a tablespoon goes a long way. Slice the avocado just before serving so it does not brown.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over a medium hob. Add the diced onion and cook for 5 minutes until softened. Add the garlic cloves and cook for 1 minute more.
Add the chipotle chillies, the tablespoon of adobo sauce and the tin of crushed tomatoes. Stir to combine and cook for 3 minutes until the tomatoes darken slightly.

Add the bone-in chicken thighs and pour in 1 litre of cold water. Season generously with salt. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 25 minutes until the chicken is cooked through.

Lift the chicken out of the broth and pull the meat from the bones with two forks. Discard the bones. Remove the two chipotle chillies if you prefer a milder broth and discard them, or leave the broth as is.
Return the shredded chicken to the broth. Add the 400g tin of drained chickpeas. Simmer for a further 10 minutes to warm the chickpeas through and let them absorb some of the broth.
Stir in the lime juice. Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt.
Ladle the soup into bowls. Top each bowl with sliced avocado and fresh coriander. Serve straight away.

attrs.cause: Chipotle chillies vary in heat level between brands and tins
attrs.fix: Start with one chipotle chilli and just half a tablespoon of adobo. Remove the chilli from the finished broth before serving. Adding a spoonful of sour cream to each bowl also cuts the heat at the table.

attrs.symptom: The chickpeas taste raw and chalky
attrs.cause: Tinned chickpeas need time in the hot broth to soften and absorb flavour
attrs.fix: Simmer the chickpeas in the broth for at least 10 minutes after adding them. If they still taste underdone, give them another 5 minutes. They should be soft all the way through with no chalky centre.

attrs.symptom: The broth tastes thin and lacks smokiness
attrs.cause: Too much water diluted the flavour, or the tomatoes and chipotle were not cooked down enough before adding liquid
attrs.fix: Simmer the broth uncovered for 10 minutes to reduce and concentrate. Add another half tablespoon of adobo sauce from the tin to boost the smoky flavour without adding more chilli heat.

content.text: Caldo tlalpeno comes from Tlalpan, on the southern edge of Mexico City. It was a traveller's soup, sold at inns along the road into the capital. Today it appears in city restaurants and home kitchens across Mexico. It is a soup for any day of the week, simple enough for a quick lunch and filling enough to stand as a main meal.
